description:
What's Brighter Than a Trillion Suns?

Episode 73 of a daily journey through the universe. 💡
Quasars: supermassive black holes feeding so fast they outshine their entire galaxies. The record holder, J0529-4351, is powered by a black hole about 17 billion times the Sun's mass that swallows about one Sun a day, and shines 500 trillion times brighter than the Sun.

segments.text: What could shine brighter than a trillion suns? A black hole, eating.
In the nineteen fifties and sixties, radio astronomers found strange points that looked like stars, but blasted out radio waves.
segments.headline: Strange radio 'stars'

segments.text: They called them quasi-stellar objects. Quasars. One of the first, called 3C two seventy-three, turned out to be billions of light-years away.
segments.headline: Quasars

segments.text: To look that bright from so far, they must be unimaginably powerful.
segments.headline: Unimaginably bright

segments.text: The answer: supermassive black holes, feeding. Gas swirling into them heats up and glows brighter than all the stars in their galaxy.
segments.headline: Hungry black holes

segments.text: In twenty twenty-four, astronomers announced the brightest one ever seen: J oh five two nine.
segments.headline: The record holder

segments.text: Its black hole is about seventeen billion times heavier than our Sun.
It swallows about one Sun's worth of gas every day, and shines five hundred trillion times brighter than the Sun.
Its light has travelled about twelve billion years to reach us. We're seeing it as it was when the universe was young.
segments.headline: 12 billion years of travel

segments.text: Next stop: Cosmic Rays. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for the next stop.
